summary.text: The disproof fixes \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and uses arbitrarily large primes as counterexamples: for prime \(p\), the only admissible integers up to \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)=2\). Choosing \(p\ge 81\) beyond any proposed threshold gives \(\sqrt{\log p}>2\), contradicting the claimed lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ divides }n\}.
\]
Equivalently, if \(P(m)\) denotes the set of prime factors of \(m\), then
\[
a(n)=\#\{k:1\le k\le n,\ P(k)\subseteq P(n)\}.
\]
We disprove the assertion
\[
\forall \epsilon>0\;\exists N\;\forall n\ge N,
\qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n).
\]
The obstruction is given by arbitrarily large prime values of \(n\).

First determine \(a(p)\) when \(p\) is prime. Since \(P(p)=\{p\}\), both \(1\) and \(p\) are counted: the integer \(1\) has no prime factors, so \(P(1)=\varnothing\subseteq\{p\}\), while of course \(P(p)=\{p\}\).

Conversely, suppose that \(1\le k\le p\) and that every prime factor of \(k\) belongs to \(P(p)=\{p\}\). There are two cases. If \(k=1\), it is one of the two integers already listed. If \(k\ne1\), then \(k>1\), so \(k\) has a prime divisor \(q\). The hypothesis on its prime factors implies \(q\in P(k)\subseteq P(p)=\{p\}\), and hence \(q=p\). Thus \(p\mid k\). Because \(k\) is positive and \(p\mid k\), we have \(p\le k\); together with \(k\le p\), this gives \(k=p\). Therefore there are no other possibilities, and
\[
a(p)=2                                                     \tag{1}
\]
for every prime \(p\).

We will also use the elementary numerical estimate
\[
e^4<81.                                                    \tag{2}
\]
For completeness, the exponential series gives
\[
e=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac1{j!}
  =2+\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}\frac1{j!}.
\]
For \(j\ge2\), one has \(j!\ge 2^{j-1}\), and the inequality is strict for, for example, \(j=3\). Consequently
\[
e<2+\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}\frac1{2^{j-1}}
 =2+1=3.
\]
All quantities are positive, so raising to the fourth power yields
\(e^4<3^4=81\), proving (2). Since \(\exp(4)=e^4\), it follows that whenever a positive real number \(x\) satisfies \(x\ge81\),
\[
\exp(4)<81\le x.
\]
As the logarithm is the increasing inverse of the exponential on the positive reals, this implies
\[
4<\log x.                                                  \tag{3}
\]
In particular, for every integer \(p\ge81\),
\[
2<\sqrt{\log p}=(\log p)^{1/2}.                            \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, (3) says \(4<\log p\), with both sides positive, and the square-root function is strictly increasing on the nonnegative reals; hence
\(2=\sqrt4<\sqrt{\log p}\). The equality with the real power \((\log p)^{1/2}\) is the usual identity between the positive square root and the one-half power.

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the proposed assertion were true. Apply it with
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
There would then be an integer \(N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1-1/2}=(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).                  \tag{5}
\]

Choose a prime
\[
p\ge \max\{N,81\}.
\]
Such a prime exists because primes are arbitrarily large. One can see the needed fact directly by Euclid's factorial argument: for any positive integer \(M\), the integer \(M!+1>1\) has a prime divisor \(p\). If that prime satisfied \(p\le M\), then it would divide \(M!\) as well as \(M!+1\), and therefore would divide their difference \(1\), which is impossible. Thus \(p>M\). Applying this with \(M=\max\{N,81\}\) supplies a prime even strictly larger than the required bound.

Because \(p\ge N\), inequality (5) applies to \(p\), and by (1) it gives
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)=2.                                 \tag{6}
\]
On the other hand, \(p\ge81\), so (4) gives
\[
2<(\log p)^{1/2}.                                         \tag{7}
\]
The inequalities (6) and (7) contradict one another.

Therefore, already for the single choice \(\epsilon=1/2\), no threshold \(N\) can make the proposed lower bound hold for every \(n\ge N\). Hence the conjecture, as stated, is false.
